web_evidence.title: James A. Michener: A Critical Companion
web_evidence.note: A scholarly book-length critical study explicitly states that The Covenant's unfolding story is presented by a third-person narrator, then surveys that narrator across the novel's chapters and family strands.

web_evidence.title: James A. Michener Writing Styles in The Covenant
web_evidence.note: An unattributed commercial study-guide page asserts first-person narration but supplies no primary-text demonstration. Its claim conflicts with the sustained quoted prose and the detailed scholarly analysis, so it is retained only as a low-tier contrary assertion.

search_log: Searched "James A. Michener The Covenant excerpt first chapter narration" and related excerpt and preview queries; Google Books exposed catalog information and a contents list but no usable sustained prose.

Searched "The Covenant James Michener point of view narrator third person" and "The Covenant Michener third-person narrator"; found the explicit whole-book discussion in Marilyn S. Severson's James A. Michener: A Critical Companion.
Searched for omniscient, alternating, multiple-narrator, frame-narrative, diary, and epistolary descriptions; found no credible evidence that the novel sustains first- or second-person base sections.
Opened the BookRags style page after its search result claimed first person; the page gave only an unsupported assertion, prompting targeted follow-up searches that continued to support third person.

Opened Google Books, Open Library, Kirkus, and Errol Lincoln Uys's manuscript-sample page; the catalog and review pages were nondiagnostic for grammatical person, while the manuscript images were not text-accessible enough to use as primary passage evidence.
person_note: The diagnostic Goodreads passages expose a nonparticipating, historically omniscient narrator: q02491 sustains an externally narrated scene and projects the children's future, while q02490 and q02498 provide broad authorial knowledge and judgment. Shorter third-person-looking passages were kept unmarked where context was insufficient, and all first-person examples occur in dialogue or embedded quotation. The scholarly whole-book analysis independently identifies the narrator as third person and describes that structure across the novel. The lone first-person web assertion is an unsupported commercial-guide statement directly contradicted by both channels. The remaining uncertainty is limited to incomplete access to authorized primary previews and does not materially challenge the classification.
